title: Aesop's Fables
author: Aesop
ru: Десять знаменитых басен о животных и людях — короткие истории с моралью.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Fox and the Grapes
chapters.text:
It was a hot afternoon at the end of summer, and the fox was hungry. He was so hungry that he could eat a horse. But there were no horses on the road. There was only dust.

Then he saw an old garden wall, and a vine was growing over it. On the vine there were grapes — big, dark, purple grapes, shining in the sun. They looked sweet. They looked cool. They looked like the best lunch in the world.

“Well, well,” said the fox, and he smiled. “Lunch is served.”

He stood under the vine and jumped. His teeth closed on air. The grapes were higher than he thought.

“Just a little warm-up,” he said. “Nothing more.”

He walked back ten steps, ran, and jumped again. This time he was close. One grape touched the end of his nose. Then he fell on his back in the dust.

A crow was sitting on the wall. She watched with great interest.

“Good jump,” she said. “Very nice. Again?”

The fox didn't answer. He jumped again. And again. He jumped from the left and from the right. He tried a running jump, a standing jump, and a jump with his eyes closed, for luck. Twenty minutes later he was lying in the dust with his tongue out, and the grapes were exactly where they were before.

Slowly, he got up. He cleaned his beautiful red coat. He put his nose in the air.

“You know,” he said to nobody in particular, “I don't really want those grapes.”

“No?” said the crow.

“No. Look at them. They're green. They're sour. Anyone can see that. Only a fool eats sour grapes.”

“They look purple to me,” said the crow.

“That's the light,” said the fox. “Good afternoon.”

And he walked away down the road, very slowly and very proudly, and he didn't look back. Not once.

The crow waited until he was gone. Then she hopped onto the vine and ate a grape. It was sweet. It was very, very sweet.

Moral: It's easy to hate the things you can't have.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Tortoise and the Hare
chapters.text:
The hare was the fastest animal in the forest, and he never stopped talking about it.

“Did you see me this morning?” he asked everyone. “Down the hill, across the river and back again — before breakfast! Nobody can beat me. Nobody!”

The other animals were tired of it. The rabbits were tired of it. The birds were tired of it. Even the trees, if trees can be tired, were tired of it.

One day the hare saw the tortoise. The tortoise was crossing the road, and it was taking him a long time.

“Hello, Tortoise!” said the hare. “Where are you going? Are you going to get there by next year?”

The animals laughed. The tortoise stopped and looked at the hare with his old, calm eyes.

“Let's have a race,” he said.

For a moment everything was very quiet. Then the hare laughed so hard that he fell over.

“A race? You and me? Oh, yes, please!”

The fox drew a line on the ground for the start. The finish was the big oak tree on the other side of the hill. All the animals came to watch.

“Ready... go!” shouted the fox.

The hare was gone like the wind. In a few seconds he was at the top of the hill. He looked back. Far, far behind him, the tortoise was walking. One foot. Then another foot. Then another.

“This is silly,” said the hare. “I can win this race in my sleep.”

It was a warm day. There was soft grass under a tree, and the hare was a little tired after all that running and talking. He lay down.

“Just five minutes,” he said, and he closed his eyes.

The tortoise walked on. One foot, then another foot. He didn't run. He didn't stop. He walked up the hill, past the sleeping hare, and down the other side.

The sun moved across the sky. The hare slept and slept. He was dreaming about gold medals.

When he woke up, the shadows were long. He jumped to his feet and looked around. Where was the tortoise? Then he heard a noise far away. The animals were cheering.

The hare ran faster than ever before. He flew down the hill like an arrow. But when he got to the oak tree, the tortoise was already there, sitting in the shade.

“Oh, hello,” said the tortoise. “There you are. I thought you were coming next year.”

Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Lion and the Mouse
chapters.text:
The lion was asleep under a tree, and the whole forest was quiet. When a lion is sleeping, everyone is quiet.

Everyone except one small mouse. She was late for dinner, and she was running home so fast that she didn't look where she was going. She ran up a big golden hill. It was soft and warm. Then the hill opened one yellow eye.

It wasn't a hill. It was the lion's head.

A huge paw came down — bang! — and the mouse was under it.

“Well,” said the lion in a deep, sleepy voice. “Dinner came to me. How kind.”

He lifted the mouse by her tail and opened his mouth. The mouse looked at his teeth. There were a lot of them.

“Wait! Please!” she cried. “Don't eat me! I'm very small. I'm not even a good dinner. I'm more of a snack. And — and one day I can help you!”

The lion stopped. “You? Help me?”

“Yes! Let me go, and one day I'm going to help you. I promise.”

The lion began to laugh. He laughed so much that the leaves fell from the tree. A mouse, helping the king of the animals! It was the funniest idea in the world.

“Go on, then,” he said, and he put her down. “Go home, little hero. You made me laugh. That's enough for today.”

The mouse ran.

A few weeks later, hunters came to the forest. They had a big net made of thick rope, and they hung it between two trees. In the night, the lion walked right into it. The net fell on him. He fought and pulled, but the net only got tighter. Soon he couldn't move his legs. He couldn't move his head.

He roared. It was a terrible sound — angry and afraid at the same time. The birds flew away. The deer ran away. Everyone in the forest heard it.

And one small mouse heard it too.

She came through the long grass and looked at the lion in the net.

“Oh,” she said. “Hello again.”

Then she began to bite the ropes. She bit and chewed, chewed and bit, with her small, sharp teeth. One rope broke. Then another. Then ten more. Before the sun came up, there was a big hole in the net, and the lion walked out of it, free.

He looked down at the mouse for a long time.

“You were right,” he said at last. “And I was wrong. Thank you, my friend.”

“Any time,” said the mouse. “But next time, maybe don't laugh.”

Moral: Little friends can be great friends.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Ant and the Grasshopper
chapters.text:
All summer long, the grasshopper sang.

He sang in the morning in the green grass. He sang at lunchtime in the warm sun. In the evening he played his violin — well, he rubbed his back legs together, but for him it was a violin — and he sang until the stars came out.

“What a life!” he said. “Sun, music, and all the grass I can eat!”

Every day, the ant walked past him. The ant was always carrying something: a seed, a grain of corn, a crumb of bread three times bigger than she was. She carried it to her home under the ground, and then she went back for more.

“Hey, Ant!” called the grasshopper. “Stop for a minute! Sit down! Listen to my new song. It's about a summer that never ends!”

“I'm busy,” said the ant. “I'm collecting food for the winter.”

“Winter?” The grasshopper laughed. “Winter is months away! Look at this sky. Look at this sun! Why are you thinking about winter?”

“Because it's going to come,” said the ant. “It always comes.” And she walked on with her seed.

The grasshopper shook his head. “Poor Ant. No music in her heart,” he said, and he started a new song.

But the summer ended. The leaves turned yellow, then red, then brown, and then they fell. The wind got colder. One morning the grass was white with frost, and the grasshopper's legs were too cold to play.

Then the snow came.

There was no grass now. There was no sun. There was nothing to eat anywhere. The grasshopper was hungry and cold, so cold. He walked slowly through the snow until he came to the ant's door. He knocked.

The ant opened the door. Behind her, the grasshopper saw a warm room and a big table full of seeds and corn. Her whole family was having dinner.

“Please,” said the grasshopper. His voice was very small. “I'm so hungry. Can you give me a little food?”

The ant looked at him. “What did you do all summer?”

“I sang,” said the grasshopper. “Every day. For everyone.”

“You sang all summer?” said the ant. “Wonderful. Then you can dance all winter.”

And she closed the door.

The grasshopper stood alone in the snow. Then the door opened again, just a little.

“Oh, come in,” said the ant. “But you're going to sing for your dinner. Every night. Until spring.”

So all winter long, the grasshopper sang for the ants. He sang very well. But he didn't sing about a summer that never ends. Not ever again.

Moral: Enjoy the summer, but remember the winter.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Boy Who Cried Wolf
chapters.text:
There was once a boy who looked after the sheep of his village. Every morning he took them up the hill, and every evening he brought them down again. In between, he sat on a rock and watched them eat grass.

Sheep are not very exciting. They eat. They say “Baa.” They eat some more. By lunchtime the boy was so bored that he wanted to scream.

So one day, he did.

“Wolf!” he shouted. “WOLF! Help! A wolf is eating the sheep!”

Down in the village, people dropped everything. The baker dropped his bread. The farmer dropped his spade. They all ran up the hill with sticks and stones, red in the face and out of breath.

There was no wolf. There were only the sheep, eating grass, and the boy, laughing so hard that he fell off his rock.

“Your faces!” he cried. “Oh, look at your faces!”

The villagers didn't think it was funny. “This isn't a game,” said the farmer. “Don't do it again.” And they went back down the hill.

A week later, the boy was bored again.

“Wolf! WOLF!”

And again the villagers came running. And again there was no wolf. And again the boy laughed.

This time the villagers were really angry. “One more time,” said the baker, “and we're not coming.”

The boy only smiled.

Then, one evening, when the sun was going down, something moved in the trees. Something grey, with yellow eyes and long white teeth. It came out of the shadows and walked slowly towards the sheep.

It was a wolf. A real one.

The boy jumped up. “Wolf!” he screamed. “WOLF! Please! This time it's true! There really is a wolf!”

Down in the village, the baker heard him. He shook his head and went back to his bread. The farmer heard him too, and he laughed. “Again? Not this time, boy.”

Nobody came.

The boy screamed until he had no voice left. The sheep ran in every direction, but the wolf was in no hurry. He chose the fattest sheep, then the next fattest, and then he had a very long, very happy dinner.

That night the boy walked down the hill with half his sheep and a lot to think about. Nobody in the village asked him what happened. They already knew. And for the first time in his life, the boy didn't think it was funny.

Moral: Nobody believes a liar — even when he tells the truth.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Crow and the Pitcher
chapters.text:
It was the hottest summer anyone could remember. No rain fell for weeks. The rivers were dry. The ponds were mud. And the crow was so thirsty that her black feathers felt like a winter coat.

She flew over fields and roofs, looking for water. Nothing. Nothing. Nothing at all.

Then, in a garden behind a house, she saw a pitcher — a tall jug made of clay, the kind people keep water in. She flew down and looked inside.

Water! There was water at the bottom. She could smell it.

She put her beak into the pitcher. It didn't reach. She pushed her head in further. It still didn't reach. The neck of the pitcher was long and narrow, and the water was low, low, low at the bottom.

“Of course,” said the crow. “Of course it's at the bottom.”

She tried to push the pitcher over. She pushed it with her wing. She pushed it with her whole body. It didn't move. It was too heavy. And anyway, a broken pitcher meant water in the dust, not water in her mouth.

A sparrow was sitting on the fence, watching her. “Give up,” he said. “It's impossible. I tried this morning.”

The crow didn't answer. She was looking at the ground. There were small stones all around the garden.

She picked one up in her beak, flew up, and dropped it into the pitcher. Plop.

“What are you doing?” asked the sparrow.

“Thinking,” said the crow. She dropped in another stone. Plop.

Then another. Plop. And another. Plop.

The sparrow laughed. “The heat is making her crazy,” he told a beetle.

Plop. Plop. Plop. Twenty stones. Thirty. Forty. The crow's neck hurt. Her wings were tired. But every time she looked inside, the water was a little higher. The stones were filling the bottom of the pitcher, so the water had nowhere to go but up.

Fifty stones. Sixty.

Then she looked inside, and there it was, near the top — cool and dark and shining.

The crow drank. She drank and drank and drank. It was the best water in the world.

The sparrow was very quiet now. He hopped a little closer.

“Um,” he said. “Can I have some?”

The crow looked at him. Then she looked at the stones on the ground.

“Bring your own stones,” she said.

Moral: When you can't use your strength, use your head.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. The Fox and the Crow
chapters.text:
A crow saw a piece of cheese in an open kitchen window. Nobody was looking. She took it in her beak and flew up into a tall tree, very pleased with herself.

It was a beautiful piece of cheese — yellow and soft, and it smelled wonderful.

Down below, a fox was walking past. He smelled the cheese before he saw it. He stopped. He looked up. He saw the crow, the branch and the cheese. And he smiled a slow, clever smile.

“Good morning!” he called. “Oh, my! What a beautiful bird!”

The crow looked down. She didn't say anything, because her mouth was full of cheese.

“Look at those feathers,” said the fox. “So black! So shiny! Like the night sky. And those eyes — like two little stars. And that beak! What a wonderful beak!”

The crow sat up a little straighter. She turned her head to the left, then to the right, so the fox could see her best side.

“Really,” the fox went on, “you are the queen of all the birds. There's only one question.” He looked sad. “Can you sing? A beautiful bird like you has a beautiful voice, I'm sure. But maybe... no. Maybe you can't sing at all.”

The crow's eyes went wide. Can't sing? Her? She was going to show him. She opened her beak as wide as it could go.

“CAAAW!”

It was not a beautiful song. It was not even a song. But that didn't matter, because when she opened her beak, the cheese fell out. Down, down, down it went — right into the fox's mouth.

He ate it in one bite. “Delicious,” he said, and he licked his lips.

“Hey!” cried the crow. “My cheese!”

“Thank you for the song,” said the fox. “And now, a little present for you — some free advice. Don't trust people who say only nice things to you. Especially when you have something they want.”

Then he walked away with cheese on his whiskers, singing quietly to himself. He had a much better voice than the crow.

The crow sat on her branch for a long time. She didn't sing again that day.

Moral: Sweet words can cost you your cheese.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. The North Wind and the Sun
chapters.text:
High above the world, the North Wind and the Sun were having an argument. It was not their first argument. It was not even their first argument that week.

“I'm stronger than you,” said the North Wind. “Everyone knows it. I can break trees. I can push ships across the sea. I can blow the roofs off houses.”

“Mm,” said the Sun.

“And what do you do? You sit there. You shine. Big deal.”

“Let's have a test,” said the Sun. “Look down there.”

On the road below, a man was walking. He was a traveller on his way to the next town, and he was wearing a long, warm coat.

“The one who gets the coat off that man is the stronger one,” said the Sun. “You can go first.”

The North Wind smiled. “This is going to take two seconds.”

He took a deep breath, and he blew.

A cold wind ran down the road. The trees bent. Leaves flew into the air. The man's hat flew off and was gone. He shivered and pulled his coat closer around him.

“Wait, wait,” said the North Wind. He blew harder.

Now the wind was screaming. Rain and ice came with it. Birds flew backwards. Dust flew into the traveller's eyes. But the man only held his coat tighter. He buttoned it right up to the top and turned up the collar. Then he walked on with his head down.

The North Wind blew and blew until he had no breath left. Then he fell back on a cloud, red in the face.

“That coat,” he said, “is glued on.”

“My turn,” said the Sun.

The Sun came out from behind the clouds and began to shine. Not hard. Just gently and warmly, like an afternoon in June.

Down on the road, the traveller looked up. The rain stopped. The air got warm. He opened his coat a little.

The Sun shone a little more.

The man opened his coat wide. He wiped his face. Then, with a happy sigh, he took off the heavy coat, put it over his arm, and sat down in the shade of a tree.

The North Wind said nothing for a long time.

“Well,” said the Sun kindly, “you were very good with the hat.”

Moral: Kindness can do what force can't.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
chapters.text:
The country mouse lived in a hole under an old tree at the edge of a field. Her home was small, but it was clean and quiet, and in autumn there were always seeds, nuts and a little corn.

One day her cousin came to visit from the city. The town mouse wore a little silk scarf and had very fine whiskers. He looked at the hole and the field, and he tried hard to smile.

“How... sweet,” he said.

For dinner the country mouse put out her best food: some barley, a few beans, a dry pea and a small piece of hard cheese. “Eat, eat!” she said happily.

The town mouse took one bean and looked at it for a long time.

“Cousin,” he said at last, “how can you live like this? Beans and seeds every day, and nothing to look at but grass? Life is short! Come to the city with me. I'm going to show you what real food is.”

The country mouse looked at her field. Then she looked at her cousin's scarf. “Well,” she said, “maybe just for a few days.”

They walked all day and arrived in the city at night. The town mouse lived in a big house, in a hole behind the dining room wall. They climbed out of the hole, and the country mouse's mouth fell open.

There was a long table, and on it were the leftovers of a great dinner: white bread, fruit, honey cakes, cold chicken, and cheeses of every colour — yellow, white, even blue.

“Help yourself,” said the town mouse.

The country mouse jumped onto the table. She took a bite of cake. It was heaven. She took a bite of cheese. It was even better. She closed her eyes...

The door flew open.

People came in, talking and laughing loudly. Then came the dogs — two big dogs, barking and running around the table.

“Run!” cried the town mouse. The two mice jumped down and raced back to the hole. They got in just in time. A big black nose pushed against the hole, sniffing, and the country mouse could feel the dog's hot breath on her face.

They waited in the dark, with their hearts beating fast. After a long time, everything was quiet again.

“Right,” whispered the town mouse. “Where were we? Ah yes, the cheese—”

But the country mouse shook her head.

“Thank you, cousin,” she said. “It was a lovely dinner. Very exciting. But I'm going home.”

“Home? To your beans?”

“Yes,” said the country mouse. “To my beans. They're not very exciting. But they don't bark.”

Moral: Better beans in peace than cake in fear.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
chapters.text:
A farmer and his wife were poor. They had a small house, a small field and one goose. The goose was white, and she was nothing special — until one morning.

The farmer went to the nest to get the goose's egg for breakfast, and he stopped. The egg was yellow. It was shining. And when he picked it up, it was very, very heavy.

“Wife!” he shouted. “Come quickly!”

They looked at the egg. They bit it. Then they took it to town, to the man who buys and sells gold. He looked at it for a long time through a small glass, and his eyebrows went up and up.

“This is gold,” he said. “Pure gold.”

The farmer and his wife walked home with a bag of money. They couldn't believe it.

The next morning there was another golden egg. And the next morning, another. Every day, one golden egg.

Soon the farmer and his wife were rich. They bought a new house. They bought fine clothes, a horse and carriage, and a big table with silver plates. The neighbours didn't know what to think.

But there is something strange about money. When you have a little, you want more. When you have a lot, you want a lot more.

“One egg a day,” said the farmer one evening. He was walking up and down the kitchen. “One. Only one. Do you know how slow that is?”

“It's a golden egg,” said his wife.

“Yes, but think about it,” he said. “There's gold inside that goose. Lots of gold. All her eggs — they're all in there, right now. Why are we waiting?”

His wife looked at the goose. The goose looked at the farmer. The farmer looked at the big kitchen knife.

“Oh, I don't know...” said his wife. But her eyes were shining too. “All of it? At once?”

“All of it. Tonight.”

So they did it. They killed the goose and opened her up, hoping for a mountain of gold.

There was no gold inside. Not one little piece. She was just a goose, the same as every other goose, inside and out.

That night, the farmer and his wife sat at their big table with their silver plates, and they didn't say a word. There were no more golden eggs. There was never going to be another one.

They had roast goose for dinner. It was the most expensive dinner in the world.

Moral: Want too much, and you can lose it all.
